item.title: Himeji Yukata Festival: The Season's First Summer Robes — Guide
item.description: The Himeji Yukata Festival, held over three nights each June, is one of the oldest and largest summer events in western Japan and traditionally the first occasion of the year for wearing a yukata. It began in the eighteenth century, when a newly arrived lord dedicated a shrine and, so the story goes, told townspeople who had no formal dress to come in their light cotton robes instead. Today several hundred thousand people fill the streets below Himeji Castle over three evenings, among hundreds of food stalls, shrine rites and lantern-lit lanes.

item.title: Toba Sea Fireworks Festival: Summer Nights Over the Bay — Guide
item.description: The Toba Minato Fireworks Festival lights up the island-studded waters of Toba Bay on a summer evening, one of the Ise-Shima region’s highlights of the warm season. Thousands of shells burst over the sea directly off the port, their colours doubled in the dark water and set against the silhouettes of the bay’s forested islets and pearl rafts, with the grand water-fireworks (suichu hanabi) fired low across the surface a signature moment.

item.title: Lake Biwa Fireworks: Summer Nights Over Otsu — Guide
item.description: The Lake Biwa Great Fireworks Festival, held on an evening in early August off Otsu, is one of the Kansai region’s biggest summer displays: some 10,000 shells burst over the open lake, their colours mirrored in the broad dark water and reflected off the lakeside towers of Otsu, drawing hundreds of thousands of spectators to the shore. Because the launches are over water with no obstructions, the shells hang huge and clear above the lake, and the setting — Japan’s largest lake, an easy ten minutes from Kyoto — makes it one of the most accessible major hanabi for visitors based in the old capital.

item.title: Nagoya Port Fireworks: Summer Lights Over the Harbour — Guide
item.description: The Nagoya Port Festival (Minato Matsuri), held around Marine Day in late July, is the city’s signature summer night: some 3,000 fireworks burst directly over the harbour basin, their colours mirrored in the black water and framed by the silhouettes of cranes and ships in one of Japan’s busiest working ports. Through the afternoon the Garden Pier area fills with festival dance parades, taiko drumming and rank upon rank of food stalls, so the evening builds from street-festival bustle to the concentrated spectacle of the finale barrages.

item.title: Gujo Odori: Japan's Longest Summer Dance Festival — Guide
item.description: Gujo Odori is one of Japan’s three great folk dances and one of its longest-running summer festivals, held over roughly 30 nights across the summer in the water town of Gujo Hachiman. Unlike festivals watched from the sidelines, Gujo Odori is a participatory dance in which anyone, locals and visitors alike, joins the circle around a central stage to dance to live music and singing, and during the famous Obon period in mid-August the celebration continues in all-night dances that run until dawn.

item.title: Suwa Lake Fireworks: One of Japan's Grandest Fireworks Displays — Guide
item.description: The Lake Suwa Fireworks Festival, held each August, is one of Japan’s largest and most spectacular fireworks displays, launching tens of thousands of shells over the lake in a show that lasts around two hours. The surrounding mountains form a natural amphitheatre that amplifies and echoes the booms, while the lake reflects the bursts across the water, creating an overwhelming sensory experience; a separate autumn ‘new fireworks championship’ also showcases innovative competitive pyrotechnics, making Suwa one of Japan’s premier fireworks destinations.

item.title: Fukui Tanabata Festival & Fireworks: A Summer Star Festival Celebration — Guide
item.description: The Fukui Tanabata Festival is part of the nationwide summer Tanabata (Star Festival) tradition, which celebrates the legend of two star-crossed lovers allowed to meet just once a year, and fills the city with colourful paper streamer decorations and bamboo branches hung with handwritten wishes. Fukui’s celebration typically combines these festive decorations with food stalls and, on the main evening, a fireworks display, making it a lively seasonal event drawing residents and visitors together for a summer night out.

item.title: Ibaraki Hanabi Taikai: Summer Fireworks Over the Water — Guide
item.description: Ibaraki hosts several large-scale fireworks festivals (hanabi taikai) each summer, with venues along Lake Kasumigaura and the Pacific coast offering particularly striking settings, as thousands of shells burst overhead and reflect on open water below. These events draw large local crowds who arrive early with picnic blankets and portable chairs, turning the festivals into full evenings of food stalls, yukata-clad visitors and community celebration rather than just a fireworks show.

item.title: Mihama Fireworks Festival: A Summer Fireworks Display Over Wakasa Bay — Guide
item.description: The Mihama Fireworks Festival is held each summer along the scenic Wakasa Bay coast in southern Fukui, lighting up the night sky over the water in one of the region’s most anticipated seasonal events. The setting over the bay allows the fireworks to reflect across the water’s surface, and the beachside location draws crowds who gather along the coast to watch the display, often combined with food stalls and a festive summer evening atmosphere in the surrounding area.

item.title: Niigata Matsuri: The Port City's Grand Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: Niigata Matsuri is the city’s largest annual festival, held each August and combining several older local celebrations into a single grand event that fills the streets around the Shinano River with parades, traditional dance performances and food stalls over several days. The festival culminates in a large-scale fireworks display over the river, drawing enormous crowds to the waterfront, and its energetic street parades feature elaborately decorated floats and thousands of participating dancers.

item.title: Toyama Matsuri: The City's Summer Festival Celebration — Guide
item.description: Toyama Matsuri is Toyama City’s summer festival, held each year and filling the streets around Toyama Castle Park with parades, traditional dance performances and food stalls that draw residents and visitors together for a lively celebration of local culture. The festival typically includes performances by local dance groups and marching bands, alongside stalls selling festival food and drinks, offering a good introduction to Toyama’s community spirit for visitors passing through the city.

item.title: Wajima Grand Festival: Giant Lantern Floats Through the Streets — Guide
item.description: Wajima Grand Festival, held each August, is the city’s largest annual celebration, featuring massive illuminated kiriko lantern floats, some standing over ten metres tall, carried and paraded through the streets by teams of local residents in a display of coordinated effort and community pride. The festival is part of the broader kiriko lantern tradition found throughout the Noto Peninsula, and Wajima’s version draws particularly large crowds given its status as the region’s biggest port town and the sheer scale of its illuminated floats.

item.title: Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival: A Summer Obon Tradition — Guide
item.description: The Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival takes place during the Obon season in August, when thousands of paper lanterns are lit along the city’s historic streets and around Tsurugajo Castle to honour ancestral spirits, a Buddhist tradition observed across Japan but given a particularly atmospheric setting here. As dusk falls, the warm glow of the lanterns against the castle backdrop and old townscape creates one of Fukushima’s most photogenic summer scenes, accompanied by traditional bon-odori folk dancing in the streets.

item.title: Sendai Tanabata Festival: Japan's Largest Star Festival — Guide
item.description: Sendai Tanabata is Japan’s largest and most spectacular Star Festival, held each August (rather than the traditional July date) since a decision to preserve harvest-season timing centuries ago. Thousands of enormous, hand-crafted paper streamers — some reaching several metres long — hang from bamboo poles along the city’s covered shopping arcades, each one taking families and shopkeepers weeks to make, transforming central Sendai into a rustling forest of colour for three days.

item.title: Aomori Nebuta Festival: Japan's Great Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: The Aomori Nebuta Festival is one of Japan’s three great festivals — and arguably its most spectacular. Each evening from August 2–7, giant illuminated warrior figures up to 9 m wide parade through Aomori City, accompanied by thousands of Haneto dancers chanting ‘Rassera!’ The final night sees floats carried out onto Aomori Bay with fireworks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City, Aomori Hours Evenings, Aug 2–7 Admission Free to watch; paid seats ~¥2,000+ Time needed 2–3 hours Best time August 2–7 (fixed dates) Highlights Giant illuminated warrior floats up to 9 m wide.

item.title: Hirosaki Neputa Festival: Fan-Shaped Lantern Floats — Guide
item.description: Hirosaki’s Neputa Festival is the quieter, more painterly counterpart to Aomori’s Nebuta. From August 1–7, fan-shaped floats (ogi-neputa) painted with mythological warrior scenes and lit from within parade through Hirosaki to the beat of taiko. The effect is more refined and mysterious than Aomori’s three-dimensional warrior figures. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Evenings, Aug 1–7 Admission Free to watch; some paid seats Time needed 1.

item.title: Kisarazu Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi & Access
item.description: Each summer, the bayside city of Kisarazu lights up the night with one of inner Tokyo Bay’s biggest fireworks festivals (hanabi) — a beloved August tradition that sends tens of thousands of shells bursting over the water. Held along the Kisarazu waterfront near the foot of the Aqua-Line, the display reflects spectacularly off the bay and draws huge crowds in summer yukata to picnic, snack at festival stalls and watch the sky erupt in colour.

item.title: Koenji Awa Odori Guide: Tokyo's Biggest Summer Dance Festival
item.description: For two evenings every August, the laid-back western Tokyo neighbourhood of Koenji erupts into the city’s largest and most exhilarating dance festival. Some 10,000 dancers in traditional costume pour through the streets to the hypnotic, driving rhythm of shamisen, taiko drums, and flutes, while up to a million spectators line the route. This is the Koenji Awa Odori — the biggest awa odori celebration outside its birthplace in Tokushima, and one of the great experiences of a Tokyo summer.

item.title: Sumida River Fireworks Guide: Tokyo's Greatest Summer Spectacle
item.description: The Sumida River Fireworks Festival (隅田川花火大会, Sumidagawa Hanabi Taikai) is the oldest and most prestigious fireworks festival in Tokyo, with roots tracing back to 1733. Over 20,000 shells launch across two competing sites along the Sumida River on the last Saturday of July, watched by roughly one million spectators packed onto bridges, riverbanks, rooftops, and into restaurants for miles around. It is one of the definitive Tokyo summer experiences — and also one of the most logistically demanding to attend well.

item.title: Yokohama Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi, Spots & Access
item.description: There are few sights more magical than fireworks (hanabi) bursting over Yokohama’s Minato Mirai skyline, their colours mirrored in the bay beside the glowing Ferris wheel and illuminated towers. Summer is firework season across Japan, and Yokohama’s waterfront — with its open harbour, parks and promenades — makes one of the country’s most photogenic backdrops. From large bay-side festivals to special event displays, tens of thousands gather on warm evenings in yukata to watch the sky light up.
